title: Ohm's law in the lab
summary: In a circuit, the voltage U across a resistor is proportional to the current I flowing through it: U = R × I. The resistance R, in ohms, measures how strongly a component opposes the flow of current.
objectives: Measure the voltage across a resistor and the current through it
Plot the graph U = f(I) and recognise a straight line through the origin
Work out a resistance from measurements: R = U / I
Predict how a resistor changes the brightness of an LED

formulas.meaning: U in volts (V), R in ohms (Ω), I in amperes (A)
the slope of the line U = f(I) is the resistance

misconceptions: Current gets used up in a resistor: in fact, the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
A bigger resistance lets more current through: it is the opposite, for the same voltage the current falls as R rises.
A battery always gives the same current: it gives a voltage; the current depends on the circuit.

activities.title: Discover Ohm's law

steps.question: If you double the battery's voltage, what happens to the current through the resistor?
steps.why: U = R × I: with R fixed, I is proportional to U.

steps.instruction: Change the battery's voltage (tap the battery) and record at least 4 measurements of U and I with the “Record measurement” button.

steps.question: Do the points make a straight line through the origin? What is its slope?

activities.takeaway: U and I are proportional: the slope of the line U = f(I) is the resistance, here about 100 Ω.

activities.title: Does current get used up?

steps.question: With two resistors in series, is the current smaller in the second one?
choices: Yes, the current gets used up
No, the current is the same everywhere
steps.why: In a series circuit, the same current flows through every component.

steps.instruction: Tap each resistor to read the current through it.

steps.question: Compare the current in R1 and in R2. What do you notice?

activities.takeaway: The current is the same everywhere in a series circuit: it does not get used up. It is the voltage that is shared.

challenges.title: Light the LED without burning it
challenges.statement: Choose the resistor so that the LED gets between 15 and 25 mA.
challenges.hint: The LED takes about 2 V, which leaves 7 V for the resistor. With I = 0.02 A, what is R = U / I?

challenges.title: Find the voltage
challenges.statement: Set the battery so that 30 mA flows through the 100 Ω resistor.

quiz.question: A current of 0.05 A flows through a 200 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it?
You increase a circuit's resistance without changing the battery. The current…
quiz.explanation: I = U / R: if R goes up, I goes down.

quiz.question: Why do we put a resistor in series with an LED?
choices: To limit the current so it does not burn out
quiz.explanation: Without a resistor, the current goes beyond what the LED can take and it burns out.
